title: Where forecasts match outcomes
subtitle: Reliability of CourtVision win forecasts against the closing reference, by sport and by game state
abstract: We measured how closely CourtVision's model win probabilities and the devigged market close match observed outcomes, in aggregate and by game state, on two graded in-game corpora: MLB (78,986 rows, 227 games) and international soccer (9,003 rows, 51 games). Both artifacts define a bin's gap as mean_y minus mean_p -- observed rate minus mean forecast -- so a positive gap means the outcome happened more often than the forecast said. A game-cluster bootstrap (1000 resamples of game_id) on 10 probability bins leaves none of the ten MLB market bins with a gap interval excluding zero (0 of 10), against 4 of 10 for the MLB model, worst at its top bin: predicted 0.9541, observed 0.6632 (n=4,753 rows, 118 games, gap -0.2909, 95 percent CI -0.4022 to -0.1822). Soccer has more significant bins on both sides (model 8 of 10, market 6 of 10) on only 51 games, so no sport-level verdict follows. Conditioned on game state, the model's largest well-sampled MLB miss is late innings (7+) at 0.8-1.0: predicted 0.9211, observed 0.6853 (n=5,037, calibration error 0.2357), against a market cell of 0.9199 predicted and 0.9405 observed (n=2,771, calibration error 0.0206) on a differently selected set of rows. The n-weighted expected calibration error the artifact publishes is all-state, not late-game: 0.079 model against 0.0591 market, over 52,646 state-labelled MLB rows. Status: the MLB corpus behind these artifacts is contaminated, so every MLB conclusion here is withdrawn pending corpus correction and regeneration and kept as a dated record; the international-soccer rows are under review.

blocks.text: How often does a CourtVision win forecast land close to what actually happened, and does that reliability hold once you condition on when in the game the forecast was made? This paper answers both parts for the two sports with graded in-game corpora -- MLB and international soccer (soccer_intl) -- and puts every model number next to a market reference number, without assuming that a shared bin label means the two numbers came from the same rows.

This is a calibration and reliability exercise only: it reports whether a stated probability matches the observed frequency of the outcome, sport by sport and game-state by game-state. It does not measure whether acting on either source's price would have produced a return; that question is out of scope here.

calibration_stability.json holds a cluster-bootstrap reliability exhibit built from data/cache/ingame_grade_joined/{mlb,soccer_intl}, dated 2026-07-23T03:21:27Z. For MLB it covers 78,986 graded rows across 227 games; for soccer_intl, 9,003 rows across 51 games. Each sport carries two independently built sets of 10 probability bins (0.0-0.1 through 0.9-1.0): one for model_prob (the CourtVision forecast) and one for market_prob (the devigged closing reference). Each bin records n (rows), n_games, mean_p (mean forecast in that bin), mean_y (observed outcome rate), gap (mean_y minus mean_p, the observed rate minus the mean forecast, so a positive gap means the outcome landed above the forecast and a negative gap below it), a bootstrapped 95 percent CI on the gap, and whether that CI excludes 0 (significant).

state_conditioned_calibration.json buckets the same style of graded rows by time_bucket (game phase, e.g. MLB late(inn7+) or soccer 75-90+) crossed with prob_bucket (a coarser 5-band split: 0-.2, .2-.4, .4-.6, .6-.8, .8-1), again separately per source. For MLB it starts from 78,986 records across 227 files and drops 26,340 rows that carry no game-state field; for soccer_intl it starts from 9,003 records across 51 files and drops 5,345. This artifact's as_of field is null in the site manifest -- date not published -- so its numbers are not dated the way calibration_stability.json's are.
Both artifacts skip one sport, mlb_clean, as a byte-identical duplicate of the mlb corpus, so the same games are not counted twice.

The aggregate bins in calibration_stability.json are tested with a cluster bootstrap: resample game_id (not individual rows) with replacement 1,000 times, rebuild the 10-bin reliability curve on each resample, and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentile of the gap as the 95 percent CI. Resampling whole games matters because rows inside one game are correlated; resampling rows would treat them as independent evidence and understate how uncertain a bin's gap is.
gap = mean_y - mean_p; 95% CI from 1000 game-cluster bootstrap resamples; significant = (CI excludes 0)

A bin label is shared between model and market, but the two bins are not paired: each side's rows are grouped by that side's own probability, so a shared label does not name a shared selection of rows. The artifact shows the difference directly -- the MLB model's 0.9-1.0 bin holds n=4,753 rows across 118 games against the market's n=5,153 across 106 games, and MLB's late(inn7+), 0.8-1 cell holds n=5,037 for the model against n=2,771 for the market. Differing counts establish that the two selections are not identical; they do not establish that the two sets are disjoint.

blocks.label: Caution
blocks.text: Because model and market bins (and state-conditioned cells) are not identically selected, subtracting a market gap from a model gap cell by cell is not a paired difference -- it is two marginal readouts sharing an axis label. Comparisons below are stated as two numbers side by side.

blocks.label: Status
blocks.text: MLB conclusions withdrawn pending corpus correction. A join-integrity check measured 2026-09-16 found that 126 of the 227 MLB game files behind these artifacts carry ticks from more than one real game, and that 27,076 of 78,986 ticks (34.3 percent) sit in a segment labelled with another game's outcome. Every MLB number below is withdrawn as a current result and kept as a dated record; the tables stay published so a regenerated corpus can be compared against them. The check found 1 of the 51 international-soccer files mixed, so the soccer rows are under review.

Aggregate reliability, MLB (78,986 rows, 227 games, as of 2026-07-23): the model's overall Brier is 0.2377 and the market's is 0.2067 (both from calibration_stability.json's per-side brier field; the model's Brier is 0.0310 higher). Of the model's 10 bins, 4 have a gap CI excluding 0 (40 percent); of the market's 10 bins, 0 do (0 percent) -- the market's MLB reliability curve does not show a single bin that survives the game-cluster bootstrap as a real miss.

blocks.caption: MLB aggregate reliability bins, model vs market, 1000-draw game-cluster bootstrap (n=78,986 rows, 227 games; source calibration_stability.json, as of 2026-07-23)
blocks.note: Bin rows for model and market are independently constructed and not paired (see Method); 4 of 10 model bins and 0 of 10 market bins have a gap CI excluding 0.

blocks.text: The model's worst MLB bin is where it is most confident: at 0.9-1.0 it predicts 0.9541 on average against an outcome rate of 0.6632 (n=4,753, 118 games), a gap of -0.2909 whose CI (-0.4022 to -0.1822) sits entirely below zero. The market's own 0.9-1.0 bin, a different 5,153 rows across 106 games, predicts 0.9483 and observes 0.9559 -- a gap of 0.0076 with a CI (-0.0354 to 0.0379) straddling zero. At the other end the model predicts 0.0512 and observes 0.2331 (n=5,127, 133 games, gap 0.1819, significant) while the market predicts 0.0527 and observes 0.0321 (n=4,176, 99 games, gap -0.0206, not significant). On MLB aggregate reliability the market is the closer-calibrated of the two, and not narrowly at the tails.

Soccer_intl aggregate reliability (9,003 rows, 51 games): the model's Brier is 0.2279 versus the market's 0.1427 (a 0.0852 gap), and both sides show far more significant bins than MLB -- 8 of 10 for the model, 6 of 10 for the market. A significant interval is a departure that was detected, not a measure of how much data stands behind it, so the market's 6-of-10 count does not diagnose the corpus. What does warrant caution is size: 51 games is a thin base for a sport-level calibration verdict, so the soccer pattern (model worse than market, as in MLB) is reported with its counts and left unsettled.

blocks.caption: MLB and soccer_intl 10-bin reliability curves, model_prob vs market_prob, from the same game-cluster bootstrap exhibit as the table above.

blocks.text: Conditioning on game state (state_conditioned_calibration.json) narrows the question to specific game-phase x confidence-band cells. The n-weighted expected calibration error this artifact publishes is an all-state figure, not a late-game one: sports.mlb.model_ece_n_weighted is 0.079 and sports.mlb.market_ece_n_weighted is 0.0591, each weighted across the early, mid and late cells alike, over the 52,646 MLB rows that carry a game-state field. Applying the same n-weighting to the published late(inn7+) cells alone gives a derived 0.1537 for the model and 0.0587 for the market, each over 13,981 rows; that pair is computed here as the n-weighted mean of the ten late-inning calibration_error values in the table below, and is not a field in the file.

blocks.caption: MLB late-inning (inn7+) state-conditioned cells, model vs market, by forecast-probability band (source state_conditioned_calibration.json; 78,986 total records across 227 files; date not published)
blocks.note: Model and market cells at the same band are built from different row sets (see Method); n differs by source at every band.

blocks.text: Late-game MLB is not a clean sweep for the market. In the 0.4-0.6 band the model's calibration error (0.0215, n=1,395) is smaller than the market's (0.0913, n=5,581); the two are close in the 0.2-0.4 and 0.6-0.8 bands. But the 0.8-1.0 band -- the model's most confident late-game calls -- is the single largest well-sampled miss anywhere in this exhibit: predicted 0.9211, observed 0.6853 (n=5,037), a calibration error of 0.2357. The market's own late, high-confidence cell (n=2,771, a different set of rows) predicts 0.9199 and observes 0.9405, a calibration error of 0.0206. In the lowest band (0-0.2) the pattern reverses again: the model's calibration error is 0.1528 (n=5,431) against the market's 0.0336 (n=3,049), so the model is worse at both extremes of confidence late in MLB games, while being competitive or better in the middle bands.

Soccer_intl's state-conditioned view runs the same direction at a coarser level -- all-state n-weighted ECE of 0.3609 for the model versus 0.2511 for the market -- on much less data: 5,345 of the corpus's 9,003 rows (59 percent) carry no game-state field and are dropped, leaving about 3,658 usable rows across game-phase x band cells. The worst of them (75-90+, 0.2-0.4, model side) has n=10 and a calibration error of 0.7883; it heads the artifact's own ranked_worst_buckets list, and at n=10 it carries too little support to read as a measurement.

sections.heading: Robustness and what would falsify this

items: If a later MLB corpus (more than the current 227 games) showed the model's 0.9-1.0 bin gap CI crossing zero, the top-bin overconfidence finding would no longer hold; the same is true in reverse for any market bin that started showing a significant gap.

The state-conditioned late(inn7+), 0.8-1 cell (calibration error 0.2357, n=5,037) has no bootstrapped CI of its own, and the aggregate 0.9-1.0 bin it lines up with is a coarser grouping (all game phases), so the two are corroborating, not identical, evidence.

Any soccer_intl claim here is testable against more games: the current counts (model 8 of 10 significant bins, market 6 of 10) would have to reproduce on a corpus well past 51 games before either count is read as a property of the forecasts rather than of this one sample.

The mlb_clean sport is excluded from both artifacts as a verified byte-identical duplicate of mlb; if that exclusion were reversed, every MLB row count and game count above would roughly double without adding independent information.

The MLB corpus behind both artifacts failed a join-integrity check measured 2026-09-16 (126 of 227 game files mix ticks from more than one game; 27,076 of 78,986 ticks carry another game's label), so every MLB figure here is a withdrawn dated record, not a current measurement.

state_conditioned_calibration.json's calibration_error is a point estimate with no confidence interval, so late-inning miss sizes cannot be tested for significance the way the bootstrapped aggregate bins can.

model_prob and market_prob bins share a label but are built independently per source, so cells at the same nominal band are not identically selected -- confirmed by their differing n and n_games -- making any cell-by-cell subtraction unpaired.

26,340 of 78,986 MLB rows (33 percent) and 5,345 of 9,003 soccer_intl rows (59 percent) carry no game-state field and are dropped, so the state-conditioned view covers an unknown-bias subset of the aggregate corpus.
The soccer_intl corpus is small (51 games aggregate; state-conditioned cells as low as n=10), so every soccer verdict here is provisional and rests on a single corpus.

calibration_stability.json is a single dated snapshot (2026-07-23) and state_conditioned_calibration.json carries no as_of date, so neither result has been checked against a later or independent season.
These are reliability and calibration measurements only; nothing here establishes that acting on either source's probability would have produced a positive return.

sections.heading: How to read this on the site

blocks.text: The interactive versions of the two tables above live in the "calibration" inspector (aggregate reliability bins, both sports, with the same bootstrapped CIs) and the "state-reliability" inspector (game-phase x confidence-band cells, both sources). The "observation-dependence" inspector explains the game-cluster bootstrap in general terms -- why resampling game_id rather than rows is the right unit when observations inside one game are correlated -- and applies beyond just these two calibration modules.

The figure above is drawn from the calibration_stability module; the state-conditioned cells come from the state_conditioned_calibration module, which the site marks partial pending a confidence-interval pass.

limitations: The MLB corpus behind both artifacts failed a join-integrity check measured 2026-09-16 (126 of 227 game files mix ticks from more than one game; 27,076 of 78,986 ticks carry another game's label), so every MLB figure here is a withdrawn dated record, not a current measurement.

state_conditioned_calibration.json's calibration_error carries no confidence interval, unlike the bootstrapped gap_ci in calibration_stability.json, so late-inning miss sizes cannot be tested for significance the way the aggregate 0.9-1.0 bin can.

model_prob and market_prob bins share a label but are built independently per source, so a model cell and a market cell at the same nominal band are drawn from different, non-identical row sets -- a cell-by-cell subtraction is an unpaired comparison, not a matched one.
26,340 of 78,986 MLB rows and 5,345 of 9,003 soccer_intl rows carry no game-state field and are dropped from the state-conditioned view, covering an unknown-bias subset of the aggregate corpus.
The soccer_intl corpus is small (51 games aggregate; state-conditioned cells as low as n=10), so soccer verdicts are provisional and rest on a single corpus.
calibration_stability.json is a single dated snapshot (2026-07-23); state_conditioned_calibration.json has no as_of date (date not published).
